newsitem.title: TOGO: Zaire antagonists under pressure at Africa summit.
newsitem.headline: Zaire antagonists under pressure at Africa summit.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, in Togo on Wednesday at a special summit on the Zaire crisis, urged President Mobutu Sese Seko's regime and advancing rebels to stop fighting and start negotiating.
Annan, a surprise participant at the one-day summit called by the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), added his voice to the mounting international pressure on the warring parties.
"I urge the parties to move to the negotiating table," he told the opening ceremony attended by 13 African presidents and delegates sent by both Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.

The rebels have now seized a quarter of the vast country Mobutu has ruled over like an absolute monarch since 1965. While the diplomats meet, Kabila's disciplined fighters are steadily advancing in Shaba, the southern province whose colossal mineral resources make Zaire a potentially prosperous state.
The summit's goal is to push the two sides into their first direct encounter in Lome, paving the way for a ceasefire and full negotiations.
Kabila's senior representative in Lome, Bizima Karaha, ruled out negotiations in the Togolese capital but did not squash hopes of some sort of an encounter with Mobutu's delegates.
The rebels have already scored a diplomatic coup by being invited to attend an OAU meeting.
But protocol was respected. Mobutu's foreign minister, Kamanda wa Kamanda, was seated with other ministers while Kabila's two emissaries sat in the gallery.
"I wish in the name of Africa to appeal to both parties to rise to the challenge of the hour," OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim said in his address.
"The presence of the two delegations offers the parties a unique opportunity to move the peace process forward with courage and determination," he said.
The rebels moved quickly on Wednesday to reject an offer by Mobutu's party to share power before elections.
"There cannot be power-sharing between us and Mobutu's people. It is impossible," their information commissioner, Raphael Nghenda, said in Kisangani.
Mobutu's Popular Revolutionary Movement made the offer in Kinshasa on Tuesday night, reinforcing the impression that the 32-year-old regime is on the ropes against Kabila.

Speculation that Kabila might be persuaded to attend the Lome summit mounted on Wednesday when he flew from newly captured Kisangani to rebel headquarters at Goma. The town has a secure airport and a fast plane could reach Lome in three hours.
But there was no sign of him at the opening attended by surprisingly few of the French-speaking African presidents accused by the rebels and their supporters of backing Mobutu.
Zaire is Africa's third-largest country with nine neighbours and the entire continent would be shaken if it disintegrates.
Kabila, a veteran enemy of the ailing 66-year-old Mobutu, says he wants to preserve Zaire's unity.
More than 1,000 U.S., French and Belgian troops are massed in Congo, ready to evacuate Westerners from Zaire if necessary.

The presidents at the opening ceremony with host Gnassingbe Eyadema of Togo were from Burundi, Cameroon, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kenya, Mauritania, Mozambique, Namibia, Sudan, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
South Africa, a key mediator on Zaire, was represented by Vice-President Thabo Mbeki.
